41982.—Although increased ventilation is one of the most
readily observed physiological responses to exercisg itis uncer-
tain how severely this hyperpnea stresses the ventilatory mus-
cles. As one approach to this question, we compared short-term
‘maximal running performance in nine subjects with and without
prior ventilatory work designed to reduce ventilatory muscle
endurance, This work consisted of 150 min of sustained maxi
mum ventilation performed isocapnically while the subjects
‘were seated. Both the level of sustained expired minute venti-
lation and the O; uptake associated with it slowly declined with
‘time during this 160-min period, On the avorago, subjects were
able to maintain two-thirds of their 12-s maximum voluntary
‘ventilation (MVV) during this long-term breathing test. ‘The
tect had no effect on subsequently measured vital capacity,

prior breathing work was reduced as compared with control
(65 vs. 76 min; P < 0.01). Subjects ceased work at significantly

icantly lower peak Op uptake (2.07 va. 8.24 l-min” step; P<

DURING VIGOROUS REYTEMIC exercise involving a large
‘muscle mass, expired minute ventilation (Vz) ean reach
levels 20 times the resting value, This enormous Vz rise
is accomplished through greatly increased activity and
thus energy expenditure of the ventilatory muscles. Are
these levels of energy expenditure great enough to fatigue
these muscles so that ther ftigue is one factor involved
in limiting heavy exercise performance (6, 10, 2)? Or, on
the other hand, do these muscles have a vast reserve that
remains largely untapped in even the most severe exer-
cise (4, 26, 28)? We performed the present study as a
‘means to distinguish between these possibilities Init we
examined tho effects of prior heavy work of the ventila-
tory muscles alone on subsequent short-term maximal
running performance. If the ventilatory muscles indeed
have a large reserve in exercise, we expected that the
‘modest reduction in this reserve induced by our ventila-
tory regimen would have no effect on running perform:
ance. In contrast, if ventilatory muscle fatigue is one
‘among several factors leading to work cessation, we ex-
pected that enhancing this fatigue by prior work would
lead to measurable decreases in running performance.

‘METHODS

Nine volunteers [5 female, 4 male; mean age 26 + 1
(SE) yz)] served as subjects in procedures that had been
previously reviewed and approved by an institutional
committee for protection of human subjects. All subjects
were active as recreational runners and none smoked.
Experimental design, Subjects were studied on three
occasions. The first was to familiarize the subjects with
experimental techniques, including treadmill running,
spirometric maneuvers such as the 12-s maximal volun
tary ventilation, and practice on the apparatus designed
‘to measure sustained maximal ventilation, The other two
experiments on each subject included 1) a control tread-
mill run and 2) the same treadmill run after prior vent
latory muscle exercise, These last two experiments were
separated by at least 2 days. To prevent an order effect
from introducing systematic bias into the results, the
control experiment was performed first in about half of
the subjects (five).
Long-term hyperpnea regimen. Subjects abstained
from food or caffeine consumption the morning of study.
Both before and 5 min after performing prolonged hy-
perpnea, subjects twice performed forced vital capacity
(FVC) and 12-s maximal voluntary ventilation (MVV)
‘maneuvers on a Stead-Wells spirometer (Collins). Sub-
Jects were seated during these tests and received contin-
uual verbal encouragement. They were then seated in a
comfortable adjustable chair with headrest; long-term
maximal ventilation was then measured. The system
‘used in these measurements has been described in detail
in the past (17). In bref, the subject breathed through a
Daniels’ valve (R-Pel) into a Stead-Wells spirometer.
Rather than allowing rebreathing from the spirometer,
however, the expired gas was channeled out of the spi-
rometer bell by a vacuum cleaner. Interposed between
the vacuum cleaner and the spirometer were valves for
flow adjustment, and a pneumotachometer (Fleisch) and
gas meter (Parkinson-Cowan CD4) for flow measure-
‘ment. Strip-chart recording of output from the pneumo-
tachometer provided a visual index of flow; actual flow
‘measurements were made each minute by stopwatch
‘timing of needle movement of the gas meter. The gas
‘meter was calibrated daily with a Tissot spirometer.
‘The subjects’ inspired gas was channeled across a 900-
cm hot water surface for warming and humidification,
Experiments using a wet-dry bulb thermometer showed
that at a constant flow rate of 100 I/min, this apparatus
heated 27°C ambient air to 33°C while increasing its
relative humidity from 40 to 95%. These procedures were
planned both to increase the subjects’ comfort (none
complained of mouth or throat dryness during the study)
